title: Reading Literature — Theme and Summary
description: Determine themes and summarize literary texts.
objectives: Determine theme from details
Summarize without personal opinion
Compare themes across texts

lessons.title: Finding Theme
lessons.content: Theme is the central message the author wants to convey; it is not the topic.
examples: Topic: friendship. Theme: True friends support each other even when it's hard.
Look for what the main character learns or how they change

lessons.title: Summarizing
lessons.content: A summary captures the most important events without retelling every detail.
examples: Include: main character, conflict, key events, resolution
Exclude: minor details, personal reactions

title: Reading Informational Text — Main Idea
description: Determine main idea and explain how supporting details develop it.
objectives: Identify main idea of a passage
Explain how details support the main idea
Summarize informational text

lessons.title: Main Idea vs. Topic
lessons.content: The topic is the subject; the main idea is the author's point about it.
examples: Topic: volcanoes. Main idea: Volcanic eruptions are destructive but also create new land.
Ask: What does the author want me to understand?

lessons.title: Supporting Details
lessons.content: Details provide evidence, examples, or explanations for the main idea.
examples: Quote relevant sentences that directly support the main idea
Distinguish relevant details from interesting but tangential information

title: Figurative Language
description: Identify and interpret figurative language including simile, metaphor, personification, and hyperbole.
objectives: Define and identify key types of figurative language
Interpret the meaning of figurative expressions
Use figurative language in own writing

lessons.title: Types of Figurative Language
lessons.content: Writers use figurative language to make writing vivid and expressive.
examples: Simile: 'Life is like a box of chocolates' (comparison using like/as)
Metaphor: 'The world is a stage' (direct comparison)
Personification: 'The wind whispered through the trees'
Hyperbole: 'I've told you a million times'

title: Point of View
description: Compare first- and third-person narrators and how POV affects the story.
objectives: Identify first, second, and third person narration
Explain how POV shapes what readers know
Compare two texts with different POVs

lessons.title: Narrator Perspectives
lessons.content: The narrator's point of view determines what information readers receive.
examples: First person: 'I walked into the room and felt afraid' — limited to narrator's experience
Third-person omniscient: narrator knows all characters' thoughts
Third-person limited: narrator knows only one character's inner life

title: Research and Informational Writing
description: Research a topic and write an organized informational essay.
objectives: Find and evaluate sources
Take organized notes
Write a multi-paragraph essay with introduction, body, conclusion

lessons.title: Finding Sources
lessons.content: Use multiple credible sources; evaluate for accuracy and reliability.
examples: Credible: .gov, .edu, published encyclopedias, peer-reviewed articles
Less credible: anonymous websites, social media, undated sources

lessons.title: Essay Structure
lessons.content: Informational essays: hook → thesis → body paragraphs (each with topic sentence + evidence) → conclusion.
examples: Topic sentence: 'The bald eagle nearly went extinct due to hunting and habitat loss.'
Evidence: cite facts, statistics, expert quotes

title: Greek and Latin Roots
description: Use Greek and Latin roots to determine the meaning of unfamiliar words.
objectives: Identify common Greek and Latin roots
Use roots to infer word meanings
Build vocabulary across subjects

lessons.title: Common Roots
lessons.content: Many English words share Greek and Latin roots.
examples: geo (earth): geography, geology, geometry
bio (life): biology, biography, antibiotic
port (carry): transport, portable, export
script (write): manuscript, scripture, inscription

title: Opinion Writing
description: Write opinion essays with clear claims, reasoning, and evidence.
objectives: State a clear, arguable claim
Support with logical reasons and evidence
Address counterarguments

lessons.title: Opinion Structure
lessons.content: Intro (hook + claim) → body (reasons + evidence) → conclusion (restate + call to action).
examples: Claim: 'Schools should have longer recess for better student learning.'
Reason 1: Physical activity improves concentration
Counterargument: 'Some say it wastes learning time, but research shows...'

lessons.title: Transitions
lessons.content: Use transitions to connect ideas and show relationships.
examples: First, In addition, Furthermore, On the other hand, Therefore, In conclusion

title: Drama and Poetry
description: Read and analyze dramatic texts and poetry, focusing on structure and sound.
objectives: Identify elements of drama: acts, scenes, stage directions
Analyze poetic structure: stanza, rhyme, meter
Interpret the meaning of poems

lessons.title: Drama Elements
lessons.content: Plays have unique structural elements that distinguish them from prose.
examples: Acts: major divisions
Scenes: smaller divisions within acts
Stage directions: italicized instructions for actors and setting

lessons.title: Poetry Analysis
lessons.content: Analyze how a poem's structure contributes to its meaning.
examples: Rhyme scheme: ABAB CDCD EF EF GG (Shakespearean sonnet)
Meter: iambic pentameter — 10 syllables alternating unstressed/stressed
Free verse: no regular rhyme or meter

title: Text Structure
description: Identify and use informational text structures to comprehend and organize writing.
objectives: Identify cause/effect, problem/solution, compare/contrast, sequence, description
Use signal words to identify structure
Apply text structure in own writing

lessons.title: Common Text Structures
lessons.content: Authors organize informational text in specific patterns.
examples: Cause/Effect: 'Because of..., as a result...'
Problem/Solution: 'The challenge is..., one approach is...'
Compare/Contrast: 'Similarly..., in contrast...'
Sequence: 'First, next, then, finally'

title: Collaborative Discussion
description: Participate in structured collaborative discussions, building on others' ideas.
objectives: Prepare for discussion by reading
Ask clarifying questions
Respond to others' ideas respectfully

lessons.title: Discussion Norms
lessons.content: Effective collaborative discussions require preparation and respectful engagement.
examples: Come prepared: annotate the text before class
Build on others: 'I agree with ___ because...' or 'To add to what ___ said...'
Disagree respectfully: 'I see it differently because...'

lessons.title: Citing Evidence in Discussion
lessons.content: Support your ideas with text evidence.
examples: 'On page 12, the author says...' to support your claim
Ask: 'What evidence do you have for that?'
